context.adhoc_rationale: Ad-hoc per ORCHESTRATOR.md section 6: the trigger is a direct human instruction to amend the pipeline's own rules. No standard workflow covers changing the workflow docs themselves. ORCH does not write documentation content (ORCHESTRATOR.md's MUST NOT list), so DOC-UPDATER produces and REVIEWER hard-gates at step 02 -- these rules bind every future run, so the producer/validator principle applies with more force than usual, not less.

task.description:
Amend the pipeline's own rules with five changes. EVERY ONE IS EVIDENCED BY SOMETHING THAT HAPPENED IN RUN WF03-ISS0106-20260821 (2026-08-21) OR ITS FOLLOW-UP ADHOC-20260821-001 -- none is speculative, and each must be written with its evidence so a future reader can see why the rule exists rather than just obeying it. That is the established style of this doc set: every hard rule in core-directives.md and every anti-patterns entry names the incident that produced it.

Write each change where an agent will actually be standing when it needs the rule. Prefer amending an existing section over adding a new one where a natural home exists. Cross-reference rather than duplicating text across files.

---

**R1 -- FAILURE ATTRIBUTION MUST BE STRUCTURAL, NEVER BY COUNT-MATCHING.**

Home: WF-02's Step 4 (TEST-RUNNER) and Step 5 (RELEASE-VALIDATOR), WF-04 where it says the same thing, and a short cross-cutting statement in core-directives.md that the workflow steps point at.

The gap: WF-02 Step 4 currently says 'Failures unrelated to this run's own acceptance criteria (pre-existing) are filed and forwarded' and WF-04 says something equivalent -- but NEITHER states how pre-existence is established. In practice agents have established it by observing that the failure set matches what a previous run reported.

That method is unsound, and this project now has the measurement to prove it rather than an argument. WF03-ISS0106-20260821's TEST-RUNNER ran the full suite TWICE on the same commit ten minutes apart and got 13 failures, then 15. The immediately preceding run (WF02-REQ066-20260820) had reported 14 on its own commit range, with two Promotion-module failures that recurred in NEITHER of the later runs, and a Check.TestTest subset of 2 against the later 3. So three runs produced three different sets. TEST-RUNNER stated the consequence explicitly: had 'matches the previously-reported set' been its criterion, its first run would have been scored as simultaneously a regression AND a fix.

The rule to write:
  * To call a failure pre-existing, show STRUCTURALLY that this branch cannot have caused it -- the failing module and its dependencies do not appear in `git diff --name-only main...HEAD` -- or reproduce it at the merge-base. Naming the specific evidence is required; 'known failure' is not an attribution.
  * Matching a previously-reported count or set is NOT evidence of pre-existence, and a count differing by one or two is NOT evidence of regression. State this in both directions, because the symmetric error is the one that hides a real regression inside expected noise.
  * A failure not covered by an existing issue record is called out AS SUCH and filed, never folded into 'the known set'.
  * Extra scrutiny is owed to any failing file that IS in the diff -- and the standard is a causal argument, not proximity. Cite the worked example: PinRebindTest failed and was in the diff, but the diff touching it was a whitespace re-wrap at lines 513-517 while the failure was at line 351 via `provisioned_tenant/0`, and re-wrapping a list literal cannot make a Postgres schema vanish mid-test.

---

**R2 -- TWO ORCH-ROLE SESSIONS ON ONE CHECKOUT.**

Home: ORCHESTRATOR.md section 7 (Parallel-run coordination), plus a pointer from HANDOFF_PROTOCOL.md's 'Do not write to registry.json yourself' paragraph.

The gap: section 7's `owned_modules` lock coordinates runs that SHARE one registry, and HANDOFF_PROTOCOL's rationale for ORCH-only registry writes cites 'a concurrent-write hazard across this project's multi-worktree/multi-host setup'. Both assume the concurrent writers are an ORCH and its subagents, or separate checkouts. Neither covers TWO ORCH-ROLE SESSIONS RUNNING IN THE SAME CHECKOUT -- and that is not hypothetical: during ADHOC-20260821-001, session WF01-TESTPARALLEL-20260821 was running in this same working tree, and it (a) wrote `handoffs/registry.json` between this session's read and its write, which surfaced only because the edit tooling rejected the stale read, and (b) committed on top of this session's commit and pushed both.

The rule to write:
  * Re-read `registry.json` immediately before writing it, every time. Append after whatever entry is now last. Never overwrite, reorder or re-serialise another session's entry, and re-validate that the file parses afterwards. The ORCH-only rule does not make the write safe on its own -- it only removes the subagents from the race.
  * The same applies to `handoffs/orchestrator.log`: append, and never assume the tail you last read is still the tail.
  * On push, when another session has unpushed commits on the same branch, push only your own with `git push origin <your-sha>:main` rather than publishing work that session may not consider ready. If that push is rejected as non-fast-forward, re-check before doing anything else -- it may simply mean the other session already pushed and your commit is on the remote, which is exactly what happened here and needed no action at all. Do not force.

---

**R3 -- 'FAILS AGAINST PRE-FIX CODE' IS TRIVIALLY SATISFIABLE FOR NEW CODE.**

Home: WF-03's Steps 2-4 note, which currently states the fail-then-pass requirement.

The gap: WF-03 requires a regression test shown to fail pre-fix and pass post-fix, which is right for a fix to EXISTING behaviour. But when the fix ADDS a module, the pre-fix failure is `UndefinedFunctionError` for every test in the file -- which proves the module is new and nothing whatever about whether the tests discriminate a CORRECT implementation from a WRONG one. A suite can fail against a missing module and still be vacuous against a broken one.

The rule to write: where the pre-fix failure is 'the code under test does not exist', the fail-first requirement is satisfied ONLY by additionally MUTATING the shipped logic and recording which tests fail for each mutant. Cite the worked example: WF03-ISS0106-20260821's TEST-DESIGNER mutated three ways -- a naive full-string OTP comparison (17/30 pass), an unstripped version suffix (24/30), warnings routed to stdout (11/30) -- so the coverage was demonstrably sensitive to each specific trap rather than merely present. Add that TEST-DESIGN-VALIDATOR must independently APPLY at least one reported mutant and run it rather than accepting the counts, and note that on that run it applied two and reproduced both exactly. Note also the isolation technique worth copying: the pre-fix side was run as `main` plus ONLY the new module, proving the tests track that module rather than anything else on the branch.

---

**R4 -- A HANDOFF'S FACTUAL PREMISES ARE CHECKABLE, AND MAY BE WRONG.**

Home: HANDOFF_PROTOCOL.md, near section 1 (claiming a handoff) or section 4, and referenced from core-directives.md's Instruction Precedence section.

The gap: Instruction Precedence makes the handoff's `task` block the highest authority for WHAT TO DO. It says nothing about the handoff's FACTUAL CLAIMS, and agents have read the precedence rule as covering both. It does not: a handoff is a record written by another agent, and docs/anti-patterns.md's 'Inheriting a claim from a record instead of re-deriving it from the source' applies to it exactly as to any other record.

Evidence -- TWICE IN ONE RUN an ORCH handoff asserted a false premise and the receiving agent was right to check rather than comply:
  (i) Step 4's handoff named the new test file with a dotted filename; TEST-DESIGNER found the repo's existing mix-task test is underscored, deviated, and REPORTED the deviation instead of silently complying. ORCH verified and confirmed the handoff was wrong.
  (ii) Step Final's handoff asserted that an add/add conflict on the renumbered issue files could not occur and, if it did, meant a third concurrent session and must be escalated. ELIXIR-DEV checked instead of obeying and showed the reasoning was false -- a rebase replays commits individually, so the intermediate commit that CREATED those files collides regardless of a later commit renumbering them. It confirmed provenance on both sides before proceeding.

The rule to write: when a handoff makes a CHECKABLE factual claim your work depends on -- a file exists, a path follows a convention, a conflict cannot occur, a count is N -- verify it before building on it. A verified disagreement outranks the handoff: report it in `result.issues` and act on what you measured, stating clearly what you did and why. This is NOT licence to disregard the handoff's INSTRUCTIONS (Instruction Precedence still governs those, and a safety/gate rule is never overridable) -- the distinction is between what you are told to DO and what you are told IS TRUE. Silently complying with a false premise and silently ignoring a correct instruction are both failures.

---

**R5 -- VALIDATE UNDER THE CONDITIONS THE PROPERTY IS ABOUT.**

Home: core-directives.md's 'Every producing step has a validating step' section, as a short addition.

The gap: that section says validators must re-derive rather than trust. It does not say that re-deriving under whatever conditions happen to be available can be worthless.

Evidence: WF03-ISS0106-20260821's REVIEWER was asked to confirm that a new toolchain-mismatch warning is unsuppressible. ELIXIR-DEV had demonstrated this in-tree. REVIEWER DECLINED to re-run that probe, on the ground that THIS HOST IS ON-PIN -- so an in-tree run exercises the match path and proves nothing about the mismatch path the property exists to serve. It constructed the real case instead: an out-of-tree directory with a fabricated off-pin version file, run under a quiet flag and with stdout redirected away. The warning still appeared.

The rule to write: re-deriving a verdict is necessary but not sufficient -- ask what conditions the property is actually about, and construct them if the ambient environment does not supply them. A green check run under conditions where the property cannot fail is not evidence.

---

Do NOT change code, tests, `docs/issues/*.yaml`, `docs/requirements.yaml`, `docs/status/`, or `handoffs/registry.json` and `handoffs/orchestrator.log` (ORCH's). Another session may be active in this checkout: if a file you need has changed since you read it, re-read and re-apply rather than overwriting.
acceptance_criteria: AC1 -- R1 is stated in WF-02 Step 4, in WF-04's equivalent step, and cross-cuttingly in core-directives.md, with the structural test named concretely, both directions of the count-matching error covered, and the 13/14/15 three-run measurement cited as the evidence
AC2 -- R1's in-the-diff-but-not-the-cause case is covered with the PinRebindTest worked example, making clear the standard is a causal argument rather than proximity

AC3 -- R2 is stated in ORCHESTRATOR.md section 7 with a pointer from HANDOFF_PROTOCOL.md's registry paragraph, covers registry.json AND orchestrator.log, covers the push rule including that a non-fast-forward rejection may simply mean the other session already pushed, says do not force, and names the ADHOC-20260821-001 / WF01-TESTPARALLEL-20260821 incident
AC4 -- R2 makes explicit that the existing ORCH-only rule does not by itself make the write safe -- it removes subagents from the race, not another ORCH-role session

AC5 -- R3 is stated in WF-03's fail-then-pass rule, requires mutation of the shipped logic when the pre-fix failure is non-existence, requires TEST-DESIGN-VALIDATOR to apply at least one mutant itself, and cites the three mutants with their measured pass counts and the main-plus-only-the-new-module isolation technique

AC6 -- R4 is stated in HANDOFF_PROTOCOL.md and referenced from core-directives.md's Instruction Precedence, draws the do-versus-is-true distinction explicitly, states that a safety/gate rule is still never overridable, and cites both worked examples
AC7 -- R5 is added to core-directives.md's producer/validator section with the on-pin/off-pin example

AC8 -- Every one of the five carries its evidence. A rule stated without the incident that produced it is a FAIL for that rule -- this doc set's every existing hard rule names its incident, and a bare imperative is exactly what agents have been observed following without understanding when it applies
AC9 -- No duplication of rule text across files: one home per rule, cross-references elsewhere

AC10 -- Only the six files in owned_modules and your own handoff are modified. Changes to existing sections are additive or amend-in-place; no existing rule is deleted, and any rule that is superseded is marked as such rather than removed

result.summary: All five rules written, each with the WF03-ISS0106-20260821 / ADHOC-20260821-001 incident that produced it (AC8). One home per rule, cross-references elsewhere (AC9). R1 (failure attribution is structural) -- canonical home is a new core-directives.md section 'Failure Attribution Is Structural, Never By Count-Matching', placed between 'Never Call a Red Pipeline OK Without a Source' and 'File Placement Rules'; it names the two structural tests (module+deps absent from `git diff --name-only main...HEAD`, or reproduction at the merge-base), states both directions of the count-matching error, cites the 13-then-15-on-one-commit vs. prior-run-14 three-run measurement, requires uncovered failures to be called out and filed, and carries the PinRebindTest in-the-diff-but-not-the-cause worked example (whitespace re-wrap at 513-517 vs. failure at 351 via provisioned_tenant/0) under its own subheading making mechanism, not proximity, the standard (AC2). WF-02 Step 4's existing pre-existing-failures paragraph is amended in place with the 4-point operative checklist and a pointer to that section; WF-02 Step 5 gains a paragraph telling RELEASE-VALIDATOR its re-run will not reproduce Step 4's set and that Step 4's attributions must be re-derived; WF-04 Step 1 gains the equivalent amendment against its overview's branch (b). R2 (two ORCH-role sessions in one checkout) -- new ORCHESTRATOR.md section 7.1 under the owned_modules lock: names the ADHOC-20260821-001 / WF01-TESTPARALLEL-20260821 incident and both its halves (registry write between read and write, surfaced only by the tooling rejecting the stale read; commit-on-top plus pushing both), states explicitly that the ORCH-only rule removes the subagents from the race and not another ORCH-role session (AC4), and gives the three rules: re-read registry.json immediately before every write and append after whatever is now last, never overwrite/reorder/re-serialise, re-validate parse; same append discipline for orchestrator.log with no assuming the tail is still the tail; push only your own SHA via `git push origin <your-sha>:main`, re-check on a non-fast-forward rejection because it may simply mean the other session already pushed your commit (which is what happened), do not force. HANDOFF_PROTOCOL.md section 4's registry paragraph gains a pointer to 7.1 rather than a copy (AC3). R3 (fail-against-pre-fix is trivially satisfiable for new code) -- new subsection under WF-03's existing 'Steps 2-4' fail-then-pass rule: where the pre-fix failure is UndefinedFunctionError for the whole file, fail-first is satisfied only by mutating the shipped logic and recording per-mutant failures; TEST-DESIGN-VALIDATOR must itself apply and run at least one reported mutant; cites the three mutants with measured counts (naive full-string OTP comparison 17/30, unstripped version suffix 24/30, warnings to stdout 11/30), the validator having applied two and reproduced both exactly, and the main-plus-only-the-new-module isolation technique (AC5). R4 (a handoff's factual premises are checkable) -- new HANDOFF_PROTOCOL.md section 1.1 immediately after claiming a handoff: draws the do-versus-is-true distinction explicitly, states that a verified disagreement outranks the handoff and is reported in result.issues, restates that a safety/gate rule is never overridable, and carries both worked examples (dotted vs. underscored mix-task test filename; the add/add-conflict-cannot-occur claim disproven by rebase replaying commits individually). core-directives.md's Instruction Precedence gains a paragraph saying the chain governs what to DO and confers no authority on factual claims, pointing at section 1.1 without restating it (AC6). R5 (validate under the conditions the property is about) -- new subsection 'Re-derive under the conditions the property is actually about' inside core-directives.md's 'Every producing step has a validating step', with the on-pin/off-pin REVIEWER example: declining the in-tree probe because this host is on-pin, constructing an out-of-tree fabricated off-pin version file under a quiet flag with stdout redirected, warning still appeared; states that a green check run where the property could not have failed is not evidence (AC7). Exactly the six owned_modules files plus this handoff are modified (`git status --porcelain` shows those six as M and handoffs/ADHOC-20260821-002/ as untracked, nothing else) (AC10); every change is additive or an amend-in-place, no existing rule text deleted and none superseded. No code, tests, docs/issues/, docs/requirements.yaml, docs/status/, handoffs/registry.json or handoffs/orchestrator.log touched. completed_at read from the clock via `date -u`.

issues.description: R1's canonical home is core-directives.md, but the operative checklist an agent needs while standing in WF-02 Step 4 is stated there in short form (the git diff command, both directions of the count error, a one-clause pointer to the 13/14/15 measurement). This is deliberate compression, not duplication of the evidence narrative -- but it is the one place in this change where two files carry overlapping wording, and REVIEWER should judge whether the WF-02 checklist is short enough. AC1 asks for R1 to be stated in all three places while AC9 forbids duplication; this is the resolution chosen.

R2 was written into ORCHESTRATOR.md section 7.1, which is an ORCH-only-audience file, while the incident's second half (pushing another session's commits) is a git-protocol behaviour that docs/agents/protocols/GIT_MERGE.md also governs. GIT_MERGE.md was not in owned_modules so it was not touched; if ORCH wants the push rule visible to the ELIXIR-DEV/FRONTEND-DEV agents that actually execute Step Final, a pointer from GIT_MERGE.md to section 7.1 is a follow-up worth scheduling.

result.next_action: Route to REVIEWER (step 02) for the hard gate on these five rule changes; ORCH commits and pushes after REVIEWER passes.
